name: Baingan Bharta
cuisine: North Indian (Punjabi; smoky mashed brinjal, also made across UP, Bihar and Pakistan Punjab)

ingredients.name: Mustard oil (sarson ka tel)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 tbsp (½ tsp for the brinjal skin + 2½ tsp for the masala)

equipment: Tongs (or two spoons) for turning the brinjal on the flame
Aluminium foil (optional) to wrap around the burner plate so drips are easy to clean; never cover the burner holes
Steel bowl with a lid (or a plate) to rest the hot brinjal so the skin loosens
Fork or potato masher, or just a knife to chop the pulp
Kadai or wide frying pan (8–9 inch)

steps.title: Wash and dry the brinjal
steps.text: Rinse the 300 g brinjal under running water and wipe it completely dry with a towel. Keep the green cap on.
steps.tip: Pick a brinjal that feels light for its size with tight glossy skin; heavy ones have more seeds and can taste bitter.
steps.visualCue: Shiny, dry purple skin, no water drops.
steps.cameraCheck: The whole brinjal on the board
steps.videoShot: Hands wiping a large purple brinjal with a towel.

steps.title: Make slits and oil the skin
steps.text: With the tip of a knife, make 3–4 shallow slits, about 2 cm long, around the brinjal. Rub ½ tsp mustard oil all over the skin.
steps.tip: Slits let steam escape so the brinjal does not burst on the flame. Optional: push a peeled garlic clove into one or two slits for a roasted-garlic taste.
steps.visualCue: The skin looks glossy all over; small slits visible.
steps.videoShot: A knife tip piercing the brinjal, then fingers rubbing oil on it.

steps.title: Place the brinjal on the flame
steps.text: Turn a gas burner to medium-high and set the brinjal directly on the grate over the flame.
steps.tip: Wrap foil around the burner plate (not over the holes) if you want an easy clean-up. Keep the kitchen window or exhaust fan open; it smokes.
steps.visualCue: The flame licks the brinjal skin, which starts to crackle.
steps.cameraCheck: The brinjal sitting on the burner
steps.videoShot: A brinjal placed over a blue gas flame.

steps.title: Roast, turning every 2–3 minutes
steps.text: Turn the brinjal with tongs a quarter turn at a time, and hold it upright for a minute at each end (stem and tip) so they cook too.
steps.tip: Medium-high works best; on a low flame the skin chars slowly and the inside may stay firm. No gas? Use the oven, tawa or air-fryer method in Section 3 instead of steps 3–4; the steps after this stay the same.
steps.visualCue: The skin is blackened and flaking all over, the brinjal has collapsed and looks wrinkled, and juices drip out; a smoky smell fills the kitchen.
steps.cameraCheck: The charred, collapsed brinjal on the flame
steps.videoShot: Tongs turning a blackened, sagging brinjal over the flame.

steps.title: Check that it is cooked through
steps.text: Push a fork or knife into the thickest part, near the stem.
steps.tip: If you feel any firm spot, roast that side 2–3 min more. An undercooked centre stays raw-tasting and won't mash.
steps.visualCue: The fork slides in with no resistance at all, right to the centre.
steps.cameraCheck: A fork pushed into the brinjal
steps.videoShot: A fork sliding easily into the roasted brinjal.

steps.title: Rest it covered
steps.text: Move the brinjal to a steel bowl and cover it with a lid or plate.
steps.tip: Trapped steam loosens the skin so it peels off easily.
steps.visualCue: Steam collects under the lid; the brinjal is cool enough to touch.
steps.videoShot: A lid placed on a bowl holding the charred brinjal.

steps.title: Peel off the charred skin
steps.text: Pull the skin away with your fingers, starting at the stem end, and cut off the stem and cap. Dip your fingers in water to remove clinging bits; don't wash the pulp under the tap.
steps.tip: A few tiny black specks are fine and add flavour. Rinsing the pulp washes away the smoky taste.
steps.visualCue: Soft, pale-brown, smoky flesh with no black flakes left.
steps.cameraCheck: The peeled pulp in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Fingers peeling the charred skin off the brinjal.

steps.title: Mash the pulp
steps.text: Mash the flesh with a fork or chop it finely with a knife. You should have about 190–200 g (about 1 cup).
steps.visualCue: A rough, soft mash with some fibres and seeds visible.
steps.cameraCheck: The mashed brinjal in the bowl
steps.videoShot: A fork mashing the soft brinjal.

steps.title: Chop the vegetables
steps.text: Finely chop the onion (70 g), tomato (90 g), ginger (1 tsp), garlic (2 cloves), green chilli (1) and coriander leaves (2 tbsp). Keep them in separate heaps.
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces; tomato finely chopped so it melts.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped heaps on the board
steps.videoShot: Overhead shot of the chopped onion, tomato, ginger, garlic, chilli and coriander.

steps.title: Heat the mustard oil
steps.text: Put the kadai on medium-high heat and add 2½ tsp mustard oil. Heat until it just starts to smoke lightly, then turn the heat down to medium and wait 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Heating mustard oil this way takes away its raw, sharp smell. If you use a neutral oil, just heat until it shimmers.
steps.visualCue: A thin wisp of smoke, and the oil turns a shade paler.
steps.videoShot: A wisp of smoke rising from mustard oil in a kadai.

steps.title: Temper the cumin
steps.visualCue: The cumin sizzles, darkens one shade and smells toasty.

steps.title: Fry the onion
steps.text: Add the chopped onion and stir on medium heat.
steps.visualCue: The onion is soft and light golden.
steps.videoShot: The spatula stirring onion turning golden.

steps.title: Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli
steps.visualCue: The raw garlic smell is gone and the pan smells fragrant.
steps.cameraCheck: The onion with ginger, garlic and chilli

steps.title: Add the spice powders
steps.text: Turn the heat to low and add ⅛ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and ¾ tsp coriander powder. Stir.
steps.tip: Low heat stops the powders from burning. If the pan looks dry, add 1 tsp water.
steps.visualCue: The onions turn evenly orange-red and smell spicy; nothing is burning.
steps.videoShot: Powders being sprinkled over the onions.

steps.title: Add the tomato and salt
steps.text: Add the chopped tomato and ⅓ tsp salt. Turn the heat to medium and cook, pressing the tomato with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: The tomato breaks down into a soft, jammy masala and a little oil shines at the edges.
steps.videoShot: The spatula mashing tomato into a thick masala.

steps.title: Add the mashed brinjal
steps.text: Add all the brinjal pulp and mix it into the masala, mashing as you stir.
steps.visualCue: The brinjal is evenly coated and the mixture looks uniform orange-brown.
steps.videoShot: The pulp being folded into the masala.

steps.title: Cook the bharta
steps.text: Cook on medium-low heat, stirring and mashing every minute.
steps.tip: Don't add water; the brinjal has plenty. Taste now and adjust salt.
steps.visualCue: The bharta thickens, looks glossy, leaves the sides of the pan, and the raw tomato smell is gone.
steps.cameraCheck: The thick bharta in the kadai
steps.videoShot: The spatula pushing a thick, glossy bharta around the pan.

steps.title: Finish with garam masala and coriander
steps.text: Sprinkle ¼ tsp garam masala and the chopped coriander, stir and cook 1 more minute. Switch off the heat.
steps.visualCue: Green flecks through the bharta; it smells smoky and spiced.
steps.videoShot: Coriander leaves scattered over the bharta.

steps.title: Serve
steps.visualCue: A thick, rough, smoky orange-brown mash with green flecks.
steps.videoShot: Bharta spooned into a bowl next to a hot roti.

reasons: a vegetable dish that is roasted rather than fried, with about 11 g of fibre, plenty of potassium, no dairy and only 1 tbsp of oil (mostly unsaturated fat). Points come off for low protein (about 5 g), so it needs dal, curd or paneer alongside, and for sodium at about 40% of the daily limit. Restaurant versions often use 2–3 tbsp oil or finish with butter or ghee, and some add cream.

researchRating.basis: a classic Punjabi home and dhaba dish with very well-reviewed recipes (Hebbar's Kitchen 4.96/5 from 240 votes; Cook With Manali 4.93/5 from 108 votes; The Foodie Physician 4.80/5 from 5 votes; Maayeka 4.60/5 from 5 votes), and it appears on "best of Mumbai" dish pages (Tripadvisor, Justdial, Zomato). Deduction because brinjal is a polarising vegetable and flame-roasting is smoky and messy, which puts some home cooks off.

storage: Refrigerate in an airtight box within 2 hours of cooking. It keeps for 2 days in the fridge. Freezing is possible for up to 1 month, but the texture turns more watery after thawing. To reheat, warm it in a pan on medium heat for 2–3 min, stirring (add 1 tsp water if it is very thick), or microwave covered for 1–1½ min, stirring halfway.
leftoverRemix: Smoky bharta toast or wrap. Spread 3–4 tbsp leftover bharta on toasted bread or a roti, top with grated cheese (or crumbled paneer) and a few onion rings, and toast on a tawa with a lid until the cheese melts. Or mix the bharta with a spoon of hung curd and roasted cumin for a smoky dip with khakhra.
burnOff: about 3.6 km of running (255 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 5.1 km of brisk walking (about 1 h at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). This is for the bharta alone; 2 phulkas would add about 2–2.5 km of running.

navratri.reason: brinjal is on the commonly avoided vegetable list along with onion and garlic (assumption: common North Indian vrat rules)

ekadashi.reason: most Ekadashi observers avoid eggplant as well as onion and garlic; some ISKCON-linked followers allow any vegetable, and for them the no-onion, no-garlic sattvik variant would fit

jain.reason: brinjal (many-seeded) is avoided by many Jains, and onion, garlic and ginger are roots

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, light and high in fibre; keep salt moderate for sehri and pair it with roti and dal or curd for a fuller meal

jain.reason: brinjal is a many-seeded vegetable that many Jains avoid, and the recipe uses onion, garlic and fresh ginger (roots)

vegan.reason: made with mustard oil; no ghee, butter, curd or cream (restaurant versions often add ghee or butter)

pescatarian.reason: contains no meat or poultry; a vegetarian dish fits a pescatarian diet

sattvik.reason: skip onion and garlic and build the masala on tomato, ginger and green peas (see Sattvik variant)

glutenFree.reason: no wheat, rava or maida, and no hing in this recipe (if you add hing, note that most hing sold in India is compounded with wheat flour)

dairyFree.reason: no dairy; avoid restaurant versions finished with butter, ghee or cream

description: A vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and dairy-free Punjabi mash of fire-roasted brinjal; sattvik (no onion, no garlic) and low-oil versions below.

variants.reason: brinjal is the base of the dish, and it is a many-seeded vegetable that many Jains avoid (Tarla Dalal; jainworld.com). For Jain families who do eat brinjal, the Sattvik variant below (no onion, no garlic) works if ginger is replaced with ¼ tsp dry ginger powder (sonth).
